steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: This boulder is volcanic in origin and yet the rest of the rock in this area is sedimentary. This area was covered by southward-moving glaciers during the last ice age.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: This boulder was probably deposited here, hundreds of miles from its geological birthplace, by a glacier.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Start with the curious fact: a volcanic boulder is sitting in an area where all the other rock is sedimentary. Something brought it here.

The author's explanation is a glacier. That story comes with a direction built in. The glaciers in this area moved south, so a glacier could only have carried the boulder down from somewhere north of here. The explanation quietly needs a volcanic birthplace to the north.

Given that, how could we argue the glacier did not bring it? Two routes. Take away the starting point: if there is nowhere to the north the boulder could have come from, the southward glacier had nothing to pick up. Or offer a different way the boulder got here.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that rules out a volcanic source to the north of the boulder, so the southward-moving glacier has nowhere to start. An answer giving another way the boulder arrived would also work. Be careful with answers about the nearest source or about distance: the conclusion only needs some source to the north, not the closest one.

notes.body: A is about "Most boulders" moved by glaciers, so this boulder can be one of the exceptions. The argument already says it was "probably" carried a long way. At most A nibbles at the "hundreds of miles" detail. It never suggests a glacier was not the carrier, which is the claim we need to attack.

A source 50 miles to the south sounds like a handy alternative birthplace. But a southward-moving glacier could not carry rock north, and B offers no other way to move it. The "closest" source being south also leaves open a farther source to the north, which is all the glacier story needs.

This is the trap that looks like it fights the "hundreds of miles" detail. It doesn't. The closest source being 50 miles north does not mean the boulder came from that one; there can be other sources farther north. And a northern source is exactly what a southward glacier needs, so C fits the explanation rather than hurting it.

The glacier explanation only works if the boulder started north of here, because the glaciers were moving south. D says there are no volcanic sources north of the boulder at all. Then the glacier had nowhere to pick the boulder up, and the author's explanation loses the one thing it needed.

This is the move to repeat: when an argument explains a fact with a mechanism, ask what the mechanism requires, then look for the answer that removes that requirement.

Whether other volcanic boulders sit nearby tells us nothing about how this one arrived. A glacier can drop a single boulder, so the absence of others within 50 miles is consistent with the glacier story. E would need to rule out the glacier or the northern source to weaken.

why: No Goal step, an Evaluate that only restated the plan, and a thin correct-answer note that did not teach the direction test.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Earth's rotation sped up over the past decade because more earthquakes shrank Earth's radius.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: A spinning object speeds up as its radius shrinks. Earthquakes increased in number and severity. Right after an earthquake, tectonic plates move toward Earth's center, shrinking the radius.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The physics is given to us, and we should not fight it: a smaller radius means faster spin. The geologist's real claim is about Earth. More earthquakes meant more plate movement toward the center, which shrank the radius, which sped up the spin.

Look at what the evidence actually shows. Right after each earthquake, the plates move inward. That is one push on the radius. It does not tell us the radius ended the decade smaller overall. If something else pushed outward at the same time, the inward movement could be cancelled.

So, given that earthquakes increased and the plates move inward after each one, how could we argue earthquakes do not explain the faster spin? Show that the radius did not actually shrink, because some other force offset the movement.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying something else pushed back against the inward plate movement, so the earthquakes produced no net shrinking of Earth's radius. An answer giving a different cause of the faster rotation would also work. Don't expect the answer to attack the skater physics; it is a stated law, and the argument's weak point is whether the radius really decreased.

notes.body: A gives an earlier case where more and stronger earthquakes came with a smaller radius. That is another data point showing the geologist's link in action, so if anything it strengthens. A weakener needs earthquakes failing to shrink the radius, not succeeding again.

The geologist's chain needs the inward plate movement to leave Earth with a smaller radius. B says that during the past decade "other geological events have counteracted the movements" that follow earthquakes. If the movement was cancelled, the radius need not have shrunk, and the earthquakes no longer explain the faster spin.

The reusable move: a cause can only explain an effect if it actually operated. An answer that cancels the cause's effect cuts the explanation at its middle link.

The skater is only an illustration of a law of physics. Whether only skillful skaters can pull it off is about technique, not about whether a smaller radius produces faster spin. Earth does not need skill to obey the law, so C leaves the argument untouched.

Knowing that the rotation rate has fluctuated for thousands of years does not tell us what caused this decade's increase. Past fluctuations could have had any cause, including changes in radius. To weaken, D would need to give a different cause for this specific change.

E says plate movement increased overall, but it does not say in which direction. More movement is consistent with more of the inward movement the geologist describes. Without a claim that the radius grew or held steady, E does not undercut the explanation.

why: Goal only restated the task in six words, and every choice note was one thin line with no test, including the correct answer.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The Industrial Revolution decreased the value that society conferred on physical labor because it enabled unskilled workers to quickly produce goods that formerly took skilled craftspeople long periods of time to produce. Computations that once took skilled mathematicians a long time to perform can now be quickly performed by moderately well-trained high school students using computers.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Our most important intellectual skills will be devalued by electronic data-processing technology [similar to the way that the Industrial Revolution decreased the value that society conferred on physical labor].

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The argument makes a significant leap. The evidence is about mathematical computations. The conclusion is about "our most important intellectual skills." Those are only the same thing if computation is one of our most important intellectual skills.

Given the evidence, how could we argue the most important skills will not be devalued? Easy: the skills we value most could be ones a computer cannot do, like judgment, writing, or the kind of reasoning tested on the LSAT. Computers taking over arithmetic would then devalue a skill, just not the important ones.

There is a second, weaker opening in the analogy. The Industrial Revolution and electronic data processing might differ in ways that matter, or intellectual skills might lose value differently than physical labor did. But the computation-to-most-important-skills leap is the cleanest target.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the intellectual skills society values most are not computational, so a computer's speed at computation does not reach them. An answer showing a relevant difference between the Industrial Revolution case and the computer case would also weaken, but expect the first.

notes.body: Computers helping to design industrial machinery tells us computers are useful. It says nothing about which intellectual skills society values most, or whether those skills are losing value. The leap from computation to "our most important intellectual skills" is untouched.

B says computation time was already shrinking before computers. That does not show computation kept its value, and it does not separate computation from the skills that matter most. If anything, it is just a longer history of computation getting easier, which leaves the conclusion standing.

When mathematicians and craftspeople hit their most productive years has nothing to do with how much society values their skills. The argument is about value conferred by society, and C changes no part of the link between computers and that value.

The evidence is about computations. The conclusion is about "our most important intellectual skills." The argument needs computation to be among those skills. D says the skills society values most "are not computational ones," so computers taking over computation leaves the most valued skills untouched.

This is the move: when the evidence talks about one thing and the conclusion about a bigger or different thing, look for the answer that pries the two apart.

Computers letting people do brand-new tasks is a fact about what the technology adds. It does not tell us whether the important intellectual skills keep or lose their value, and it does not say those skills are non-computational. The argument's gap remains open.

why: Explicit-Standard register: dashes, padded notes, no Goal step, and A and E notes claimed a strengthening effect the choices do not have.

steps.label: Evidence (because)
steps.body: Sonora was sculpted by Barajas’s assistants, working from three sketches Barajas drew in preparing to sculpt the statue.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: The statue probably looks very much like it would have looked if Barajas had lived to complete it.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The evidence in this argument is pretty flimsy, leaving it open to several objections. Were the assistants skilled enough to sculpt Sonora the way Barajas would have? Did three sketches give them enough information about how Barajas wanted the finished statue to look? And what if Barajas's statues often ended up looking quite different from the early sketches?

That last one is the sharpest. The whole argument leans on the sketches standing in for the finished statue. Given that the assistants followed the sketches, how could the statue still look different from what Barajas would have made? It could, if the sketches were only an early draft of an idea that Barajas would have kept changing.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer showing that three sketches do not capture what Barajas's finished statue would have looked like, for example because Barajas's designs usually changed a lot after the first sketches. An answer showing the assistants could not carry out Barajas's style would also work. Weaken answers don't always match the prediction, so test each one: does it make the resemblance less likely?

notes.body:
The argument treats three sketches as a reliable picture of the finished statue. A says Barajas's ideas "were revised substantially throughout a series of dozens of preliminary sketches." Three sketches are then an early draft, not the final design, and the statue Barajas would have finished could look very different.

The move to repeat: find the piece of evidence the conclusion leans on, then look for the answer that shows it is not a reliable guide.

One assistant who helped plan Sonora did not sculpt it. We don't know how many other assistants planned it, and the sculptors still had Barajas's own sketches. Losing one person might matter a little or not at all, so B gives no clear reason the statue looks different.

The choice is hedged twice: Sonora is made "partly" of materials Barajas did not "frequently" use. So Barajas sometimes used them, and they may be a small part of the statue. Unusual materials also need not change how the statue looks. The effect on resemblance is too uncertain to weaken.

If Barajas "always worked from sketches," the assistants were following Barajas's own process. That makes the sketches look like a better guide, which strengthens the argument rather than weakening it.

Taking longer than Barajas would have says nothing about how the statue looks. Slower work could just mean careful work. The conclusion is about resemblance, so a difference in speed does not touch it.

why: Explicit-Standard register with dashes and padding, a gendered pronoun in the breakdown, and a Goal that named no expected answer.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Our country needs as much capital as possible from overseas investors in order to sustain our economy.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion (Hence)
steps.body: We cannot afford any reduction in the amount of capital that these investors have invested here.

steps.label: Main Conclusion (Therefore)
steps.body: To sustain our economy, we should pass laws making it much more difficult for overseas investors to remove their capital.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
There isn't a huge gap in logic between needing as much capital as possible (the evidence) and not wanting any reduction in the existing amount of capital (the intermediate conclusion).

But there is a significant gap between the intermediate conclusion and the main conclusion. Wanting to avoid any reduction in investments does not automatically support the idea that we should pass laws making it more difficult for investors to remove their capital.

This main conclusion is a recommendation. Plans and recommendations tend to be vulnerable to a variety of objections, and the correct answer to a Weaken question might focus on any one of them. It helps to think about the kinds of objections that this argument is particularly vulnerable to.

For example, a recommendation might have the opposite effect. Maybe these laws would discourage investors from making future investments, which would prevent us from acquiring "as much capital as possible." Or there might be some reason why this particular recommendation can't be implemented, or won't be effective. Maybe these types of laws are almost impossible to enforce, and therefore tend to be ineffective.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that suggests the recommendation might backfire or be impossible to implement correctly. But, since objections can take many forms, read answers with an open mind. We want to notice if one attacks the recommendation in another way.

notes.body: Diversifying investments across industries is a separate goal. The country could need diversification and still benefit from keeping overseas capital in place. A gives no reason the proposed laws would fail or backfire, so the recommendation survives.

The economist wants "as much capital as possible" from overseas investors. B says these laws "would strongly discourage them from investing any additional capital." The laws might stop some money from leaving, but they would choke off new money coming in. The plan works against its own goal.

This is the standard way to attack a recommendation: show it backfires on the very thing it was meant to protect.

Growth was highest when overseas capital was highest. That supports the premise that the country needs overseas capital, which the argument already grants. Confirming the premise gives no reason to doubt the laws, so if anything C strengthens.

D is the tempting one, because it suggests the laws are not fully effective. But "not entirely prevented" leaves room for the laws to stop most capital from leaving, which would still help the economist. To weaken a plan, we want it to fail or backfire, and D shows neither.

The country passed some restrictions two years ago, but E tells us nothing about what happened next. If they worked, the argument is helped; if they backfired, it is hurt. With no outcome, E has no clear effect.

why: Breakdown was sound, but the choice notes were in the explicit-Standard register with dashes and repetition, and the D trap did not get a clear test.

steps.label: Curious Fact
steps.body: Why are the ant-hosting orchids of a given species healthier than the orchids that don't host ants?

steps.label: Provided Explanation
steps.body: The ants store organic matter in the orchids' roots. That matter gives the orchids extra nutrients, and the extra nutrients make them healthier.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Our task is an alternate explanation for the correlation between housing ants and being a healthier orchid. We are not asked to attack the nutrient story, only to give another story that would also explain the fact.

Whenever we need an alternate explanation for a correlation, check the usual routes.

Reverse cause: maybe the healthier orchids come first, and ants prefer to move into healthy roots.

Third factor: maybe something that comes with the ants, such as a damp spot in the soil, is what makes those orchids healthier.

Same cause, different mechanism: maybe the ants do help the orchids, just not through nutrients. They could protect the roots, for example.

So look for an answer that explains why ant-housing orchids are healthier without relying on the stored organic matter. An answer that only makes the nutrient story weaker, or adds detail to it, is not an alternative.

notes.body: Microscopic organisms breaking down the stored organic matter is a detail of how the nutrients might reach the orchid. That fills in the author's own explanation rather than replacing it. We need a different reason the orchids are healthier.

B is tempting because it makes the nutrient story look shakier: the stored matter has the same nutrients as the soil. But the stem asks for an alternative explanation, and B gives no other reason ant-housing orchids are healthier. Casting doubt on one explanation is not offering another.

C keeps the ants as the cause but changes how they help. The ants "prey on an insect species whose members eat the orchids’ roots." Orchids with ants lose fewer roots to those insects, so they are healthier for a reason that has nothing to do with stored nutrients. That is a full second explanation for the same fact.

The move to repeat: on alternate-explanation questions, look for a different path from the same two facts, here the ants and the orchids' health.

D tells us one thing the ants don't do: they don't pollinate the flowers. A thing the ants don't do cannot explain why their orchids are healthier. D removes one possible explanation and offers nothing in its place.

E points the wrong way: plants that harbor insects tend to be more prone to disease and rot. That would make the ant-housing orchids' good health more surprising, not less. It is also about "Most plant species," not this orchid. No explanation here.

why: Explicit-Standard register: dashes in the Goal and correct note, a garbled question mark in the provided explanation, and wrong-answer notes without the test.

steps.label: Opposing Evidence
steps.body: During a study, a group of subjects receiving vitamin C had less severe acne than did the control group, which received a placebo.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Half of the subjects in each group knew which kind of pill they were given. Among those who could not tell [which pill they were given], no difference in the severity of acne was found between the two groups.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: We can tentatively conclude that vitamin C has no real benefit in reducing the severity of acne.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Let's be clear about which groups are being compared. Overall, the vitamin C group had less severe acne than the placebo group. Then the scientists split each group in half: subjects who knew which pill they had, and subjects who could not tell.

Among the subjects who could not tell, there was no difference in acne. So the overall gap came from the subjects who knew. The author's reading: knowing you got the vitamin made the difference, not the vitamin. The blind comparison is treated as the fair test, and that test found nothing.

That reading depends on the blind comparison really being fair. Finding "no difference in the severity of acne" means both blind groups ended up in the same place during the study. It only shows the vitamin did nothing if both groups started in the same place too.

Given that, how could we argue vitamin C did help? Suppose the vitamin C subjects started with worse acne. Then ending up equal to the placebo group means they improved more. The "no difference" result would hide a real benefit.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer showing the blind comparison was not a fair one: most likely, that the vitamin C subjects started out with worse acne than the placebo subjects, so matching them during the study is evidence of improvement. More generally, any answer giving evidence that vitamin C actually helped the blind subjects will weaken.

notes.body:
The conclusion rests on the blind comparison showing "no difference in the severity of acne" between the groups. A says the vitamin C subjects "had a history of suffering from more severe acne" than the placebo subjects. If the vitamin C group started worse and ended up equal, it improved more than the placebo group did. That is a benefit, hidden inside a result of no difference.

The reusable test for study arguments: before trusting a comparison, ask whether the two groups started out alike. If they didn't, equal results can mean unequal effects.

B rules out vitamin C subjects taking extra doses on their own. That closes a loophole, but it doesn't make the blind comparison less trustworthy, and it gives no evidence that the vitamin worked. The no-difference result among blind subjects stands as it was.

Acne below the national average describes both groups alike. The argument compares the groups inside the study, so a shared fact about both doesn't change the comparison. C gives no reason to think the vitamin C group would have been worse off without the pills.

D is the most tempting trap. If placebo subjects got vitamin C from food, the control group was not vitamin-free. But D says only that "Some" placebo subjects ate vitamin C-rich foods, which is an ordinary diet and could just as easily describe the vitamin C group. Nothing suggests the food matched the pill's dose or that it happened among the blind subjects. So D barely dents the comparison, while A gives direct evidence that the vitamin helped.

Some subjects who knew they had placebos skipped them. Those subjects are in the half that knew, which the conclusion already sets aside. And a placebo has no active ingredient, so taking it or not changes nothing about vitamin C. The blind comparison is untouched.

why: Evaluate misdescribed the argument as an unproven-vs-false flaw and overstated the data, the D note contradicted itself, and the register used dashes throughout.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Winchester can't afford to keep its several small branch libraries supplied with a wide selection of current books. If the branch libraries were closed, then Winchester could afford to open one large library. The large library could carry broader and more current selections [of books].

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Winchester would better meet its residents' needs by closing its small branch libraries and opening one larger, well-supplied library.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The conclusion makes a recommendation about building a new library. It does this by introducing a new concept of better meeting residents' needs. A couple of assumptions are required to reach this conclusion. First, the argument assumes that one large library would better meet residents' needs than several smaller ones. We can easily envision a situation where it's convenient for residents to visit the branch libraries that are close to their neighborhoods, while a single main library would be farther away and therefore less accessible. The argument also assumes that a broader and more current selection of books would better meet residents' needs. But people use libraries for many reasons other than borrowing books. Libraries often have computers, study rooms, and meeting rooms that residents can use. Libraries often offer classes and events. And people are likely to borrow older books from libraries, not just current ones.

So, given that one big library would have better books, how could we argue residents would be worse off? Show that the new library would fail them in some other way, most likely because they could not easily get to it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: A correct answer is likely to focus on one of these unintended consequences of closing the branches, a cost that would stop one large library from serving residents better than the existing branches. The likeliest target: residents could not easily reach the single new library.

notes.body: Residents who never use the branches because of irregular hours lose nothing when the branches close. If anything, A gives another reason the branches are failing residents. It shows no way the single large library would serve them worse.

Complaints about the book selection at the branches back up the argument's premise that the branches are poorly supplied. That makes a bigger, better-stocked library sound more welcome, so B strengthens rather than weakens.

The argument assumes better books means better service. C says "The only possible site for a new library is not readily accessible to most Winchester residents." A library most residents can't easily reach does not meet their needs, however good its books are. The branches, poorly stocked as they are, at least sit nearby.

The move to repeat: when an argument recommends a plan for one benefit, look for the cost it ignored.

The argument already says closing the branches would let Winchester afford the large library. A "significant amount of money" is consistent with that. D would weaken only if the cost exceeded what Winchester could afford, and it doesn't say so.

If each branch tries to serve the whole township, the branches duplicate each other's job, which makes one central library sound sensible. E gives no reason the residents would lose anything by consolidating, so it does not weaken.

why: Breakdown was mostly sound, but the Evidence left out the first premise, the Goal named no specific answer, and the notes were formulaic, with E arguing about a stronger hypothetical choice.
